settings.text: Power dressing is a jewelry problem

The suit is easy. The jewelry is where New York women give themselves away — too little and you look unfinished in a boardroom; too much and you look like you dressed for a gala at noon. Corporate women here need a weekday uniform that survives a 12pm lunch in Midtown, a 4pm deck, and a 7pm drink without a costume change.

Zoom still exists. Tiny specks disappear; chandelier drops look like you are presenting from a party. A round or emerald-cut stud with presence — lab-grown is how you get the size without the budget fight — is the one piece partners notice without commenting on.

A tennis or station necklace under an open collar is the corporate equivalent of good stationery. It finishes a white shirt. It does not compete with a statement lapel. If you only buy one piece this quarter, make it this — natural or Peaceful Diamonds, so long as the set is tight and the metal matches your other daily gold.

A stack of slim bands, or one stone that sits low. High-profile cocktail rings belong at Bemelmans, not on a trackpad. If you are signing anything, the jewelry should still look like you when your hands are on the table.

Before you buy, picture The Grill, a corner table at The Modern, or a hotel dining room off Park. If the piece would embarrass you across from a client — too loud, too bridal, too much branding — skip it. Laura's rule in the Diamond District was always the same: buy once, wear constantly, hand it down.
